Meeting header: 2025-06-10 09:00 PT | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Michael Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Kapoor (VP Eng, Luminis), Sophie Tran (ML Eng), Marcus Lee (Platform)

Summary: quick POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscaling strategy for a 6-week pilot. Customer provided QPS targets, latency SLOs, and sequence length distribution. Discussed reserved GPU sizing, burst capacity model, fallback to smaller model variants or CPU-only during sustained overload, and how Redwood handles KV cache / prefix caching. Agreed to run a benchmark next week and deliver a written POC proposal and pricing.

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got 55 minutes, agenda is sizing the POC, success criteria, and what benchmarking we'll run. Michael and I will cover the infra part.
[00:18] Ravi: Great, thanks. Our key ask is to validate performance for our summarize-and-search feature. We want p95 latency under 400ms on a 2k token seq, and sustain ~80 qps with spikes to 200 qps for a few minutes.
[00:35] Michael: Okay that's helpful. Can you confirm the model family and whether you're using context windows with long histories?
[00:44] Sophie: We're planning to use an open LLM similar to Llama2-70B (we've quantized to 4-bit for prod), average sequence length is 1.2k tokens, 10% of requests hit 2k+ tokens. 60% are simple extractive prompts with short completion.
[01:05] Marcus: Also, we need VPC peering and strict egress control - can't allow public internet egress from inference nodes.
[01:12] Aisha: Understood. For the POC we usually recommend reserving baseline GPUs and enabling burst capacity to handle spikes. For your numbers I'd expect to propose 4 reserved A100-class GPUs for steady state and 2-4 burst nodes to handle peak - but we'll validate with a benchmark.
[01:35] Michael: A couple clarifications - what's your concurrency per request? Is batching acceptable? How tolerant are you to microsecond variability?
[01:44] Sophie: We can batch up to 4 requests, but prefers lower latency for conversational paths. Concurrency per process is ~8 workers.
[01:52] Michael: Great. For the benchmark we'll run: throughput test (qps sweep), p95/p99 latency at target seq lengths, and a fault-injection test where we simulate node loss and force fallback to a smaller model variant.

[02:10] Sophie: How does Redwood's autoscaler decide when to run burst GPUs? Is it instant or does it ramp?
[02:18] Michael: It depends on policy. We do a fast scale-up for immediate bursts (spinning up pre-warmed nodes if you enable burst pool) - typically seconds to a minute if warmed, otherwise a few minutes cold. We offer two modes: pre-provisioned burst (reserved warm nodes you pay less for than full dedicated) and on-demand cloud-backed nodes. The pre-warmed option is recommended for your 200 qps spikes.
[02:42] Ravi: What's the cost tradeoff on pre-warmed? If we reserve 2 pre-warmed GPUs that barely get used, is that expensive?
[02:50] Aisha: We'll show exact numbers in the proposal but rough math: reserved capacity has committed monthly cost; pre-warmed burst is mid-way between on-demand and reserved, you pay for the node being warm but it's cheaper than a full-time reserved GPU. Also we can configure maximum burst budget to cap spend.

[03:08] Marcus: Suppose the burst threshold is hit and there are no warm nodes and cloud capacity is delayed. What's the fallback policy?
[03:16] Michael: Good question. We typically configure two fallback tiers: automatic fallback to a compatible, smaller model variant (e.g., from 70B to 13B quantized), and then a final fallback to CPU inference for low-priority traffic. We can also route traffic by priority: user-facing real-time goes to reserved/burst pool first; background jobs go to a cheaper path.
[03:36] Sophie: Is model variant fallback lossy? Will quality drop significantly?
[03:40] Michael: There will be degradation, we recommend a canary set of prompts to quantify quality delta during the benchmark. As part of the POC we run A/B quality checks using your eval prompts so you can set acceptable thresholds.

[03:56] Ravi: For success criteria: we want p95 < 400ms for 2k tokens for at least 90% of test runs, throughput 80 sustained qps, and successful fallbacks without errors. Any objections?
[04:06] Aisha: Sounds reasonable. We'll add an SLO for availability during the POC - target 99.5% up for the inference path.

[04:20] Michael: On sizing - with 4 A100 GPUs in reserved pool, and batching of 2-4, we can hit ~80 qps for your mix depending on quantization and kernel performance; if we see lower throughput in the benchmark we scale to 6 reserved for the POC and use burst for spikes. Exact numbers depend on real bench.

[04:40] Sophie: On data handling: we need to ensure no customer PII is persisted and logs are forwarded to our SIEM. Can Redwood restrict token logging?
[04:48] Aisha: Yes, we have options: token-level retention policies, and can disable request logging. We'll include SOC2 docs and KMS integration notes.

[05:00] Marcus: Network: we require privatelink/VPC peering and internal NAT for outbound only to approved endpoints. Is that supported for the POC?
[05:08] Michael: Yes, for Private deployments we can do VPC peering. For hosted POC we can do a peered endpoint; for private POC we'd spin up a customer-dedicated control plane. We'll outline the network plan in the proposal.

[05:25] Ravi: What's the timeline to stand up the POC infra and run benchmarks?
[05:30] Aisha: Typical POC timeline is 4-6 weeks: week 0-1: finalize scope & infra, week 2: deploy & baseline, week 3: run benchmarks and iterate, week 4: quality evals and results review. If you want an accelerated 3-week run we can do that but it requires more reserved capacity up front.

[05:50] Sophie: For the benchmark harness, we have a replay of production traces but need a lightweight version for the POC. Michael, can you accept a sample trace and convert it?
[05:58] Michael: Yes, send a sanitized trace (Sophie will do) and we'll map request distribution into our harness. We'll also provide a small docker runner to run locally.

[06:12] Aisha: Let's talk cost guardrails: we can set per-minute or per-day spend caps, and also a hard throttle if the POC reaches a spend threshold you set. That avoids surprise bills.

[06:22] Marcus: Good. Can we also enforce routing policies so certain keys always go to reserved pool and others to burst?
[06:28] Michael: Yes, routing rules are configurable - by API key, route, or request priority header. We'll show examples in the proposal.

[06:40] Sophie: Any limitations around kv cache and long-running chat sessions?
[06:45] Michael: KV cache is supported, but on multi-node scaling we need to ensure shared KV cache or warm-start behavior. For highest throughput with long contexts we recommend sticky sessions to a pod with KV cache, or use our distributed KV caching which we can enable for the POC. Small gotcha - some early quant kernels can't spill KV cache efficiently so we'll validate in bench.

[07:05] Ravi: Ok walk me through a failure scenario: high sustained traffic, reserved full, burst exhausted, model fallback used, customer still sees slow responses - what telemetry will we provide?
[07:16] Michael: We expose per-token latency, per-route breakdown, number of active GPUs, cache hit rates, and fallback events. We also emit traces with request IDs so you can correlate with your logs.

[07:28] Aisha: We'll also set automatic alerts on p95 latency and error rate; if thresholds hit we can trigger a rollback to a smaller model or throttling.

[07:38] Sophie: For the benchmark, can we capture quality metrics automatically? We have a set of 500 eval prompts and expect Rouge/BLEU-like scoring and some human judgments for a subset.
[07:47] Michael: Yes we'll run the eval set and produce a quality delta report between model variants. We'll also tag outputs with a quality score for easy A/B.

[08:02] Ravi: Sounds good. A couple of smaller Qs: how do you handle model pinning and rollouts during the POC? If we iterate models, can we do canary?
[08:10] Aisha: Yes, canary rollouts are supported - route a small % of traffic to the new model, monitor quality and latency, then increase. We'll manage that via the console and provide rollout plans.

[08:27] Marcus: Anything we should be worried about with quantization? Our team already converted to 4-bit but want to make sure backend kernels are optimized.

[08:36] Michael: Some kernels are better-optimized on certain GPU families. We'll run kernel-compatibility checks; if needed we'll recommend a different GPU type or a different quantization profile for the POC.

[08:50] Sophie: Ok next steps recap?
[08:54] Aisha: We'll send a written POC proposal with recommended reserved size (initially 4 reserved A100 equiv, 2 pre-warmed burst), pricing, and timelines. Michael will share benchmark harness + instructions. Sophie will provide sanitized trace and eval prompts. Marcus will confirm network constraints. We'll schedule benchmark run next Wednesday morning - does that work?
[09:14] Ravi: Yes that works.

[09:20] Aisha: Anything else?
[09:23] Marcus: One ask - can you include a fallback SLA for the POC where you guarantee no silent failures and all fallbacks logged?
[09:30] Aisha: Yes we'll include explicit fallback logging commitments.

[09:35] Sophie: Great. Thanks everyone.

[09:38] Aisha: Thanks - we'll follow up with docs and the proposal. End call.
